summary: Gives guidelines for B2BUAs that sit on the media path so RTCP works end to end, avoiding degraded communication when they split sessions.

plainLanguage.summary: A relay in a phone call must pass along the quality reports, not hide them.

questions: why does rtcp break through a b2bua
how should a b2bua handle ssrc rewriting
can a b2bua work with srtp
subtitle: Rules for SIP back-to-back user agents so that RTCP quality feedback still reaches the right endpoint.

tldr.problem: A B2BUA on the media path splits a call into separate RTP sessions and may rewrite SSRCs and sequence numbers, so relayed RTCP feedback refers to identifiers the receiver does not know and gets dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts B2BUAs into Media Relay, Media-aware Relay and Media Terminator, and says how each must handle SDP attributes and rewrite RTCP packet fields to match any changes it made to RTP.
tldr.outcome: Followed consistently, loss reports, congestion feedback and retransmission requests survive the B2BUA. Secure RTP limits this: only the plain Media Relay case can be handled properly.

facts.label: Secure RTP
facts.value: Only the Media Relay case is properly addressed

today: RFC 8079 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with B2BUAs on the Media Path
sections.content:
A SIP Back-to-Back User Agent (B2BUA) acts as both a user agent server and a user agent client. Many also sit on the media path and handle RTP and RTCP, which splits a call into separate RTP sessions, one per side. This breaks the end-to-end nature of the protocols. RTP packets are easy to relay, but RTCP carries feedback on call quality that depends on consistent identifiers.

The RFC's example has Alice and Bob with a B2BUA between them. Alice sends with SSRC1 and the B2BUA rewrites it to SSRC3 for Bob. Bob sends with SSRC4, rewritten to SSRC2 for Alice. If Alice reports packet loss using SSRC2 and SSRC1 and the B2BUA relays that blindly, Bob knows only SSRC3 and SSRC4, so he drops the feedback. He may then flood Alice with more media than she can handle or fail to retransmit lost packets, and the call may even end.
sections.plainLanguage: The middle person gave everyone new nicknames. When Alice complains using the old nicknames, Bob has no idea who she means and ignores her.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Media-Handling B2BUA
sections.content:
Building on RFC 7092, the document separates B2BUAs into three categories and gives guidance for each. It adds to what RFC 3550 and RFC 7667 already require for particular topologies.

  • Media Relay: forwards RTP and RTCP without inspecting or changing them. It is an RTP Transport Translator.
  • Media-aware Relay: inspects RTP and RTCP and may change headers, but does not change payloads such as by transcoding. It is an RTP Translator.
  • Media Terminator: terminates media itself and can transcode or originate RTP. It is an RTP Media Translator.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of middle person: one who just passes notes along, one who reads and relabels them, and one who writes brand new notes.

sections.title: Media Relay Rules
sections.content:
Because a Media Relay leaves headers alone, SSRC mismatches do not arise from packet rewriting. They can still arise from the session description. If the B2BUA builds a new SDP with wrong ssrc attributes, or advertises NACK support the original INVITE did not, endpoints see mismatches.

A Media Relay SHOULD therefore forward all SSRC- and RTCP-related SDP attributes, including rtcp-fb and rtcp-xr-attrib. Attributes that describe the immediate peer, such as rtcp (the expected RTCP port), must be rewritten, and other attributes SHOULD be forwarded.

For RTP/RTCP multiplexing, a relay that cannot parse RTP and RTCP SHOULD reject it by removing rtcp-mux. One that can parse them and sees no Payload Type overlap SHOULD negotiate it.

Unchanged RTCP can also leak information such as domain names in CNAME items, and CNAMEs that contain IP addresses may collide behind a NAT. A B2BUA MAY rewrite CNAMEs, and if it does it MUST generate new ones following RFC 7022.
sections.plainLanguage: A note-passer who never touches the notes still has to describe the call honestly when setting it up, and must not pass along notes that name only the person next door.

sections.title: Media-aware Relay Rules
sections.content:
A media-aware B2BUA that changes SSRCs, sequence numbers or similar RTP data MUST change the same information coherently in RTCP. It SHOULD NOT randomly drop or forward feedback of the same type within a session, because gaps confuse recipients. If it drops a message it cannot parse, it SHOULD NOT drop the whole compound RTCP packet, and it MUST advertise its RTCP support in SDP accurately.

Packet by packet, the rules are:

  • SR and RR (RFC 3550): update the sender SSRC and any SSRCs in Report Blocks. If the base sequence number changed, reflect it in the extended highest sequence number received.
  • SDES, BYE and APP: update any changed SSRCs.
  • XR (RFC 3611): same SSRC rules, plus begin_seq and end_seq if sequence numbers changed.
  • Feedback messages (RFC 4585): update the packet sender and media source SSRCs, but not a media source SSRC originally set to zero. For NACK, rewrite the Packet ID if sequence numbers changed. For TMMBR, TMMBN, FIR, TSTR, TSTN and VBCM (RFC 5104), rewrite the extra SSRC in the control information.
  • REMB: not standardized at the time of writing; it breaks across a B2BUA that changes SSRCs unless the SSRCs in it are changed too.

PLI, SLI and RPSI need nothing beyond the generic feedback rules. In SDP, a B2BUA that changes an SSRC MUST update the matching ssrc attributes and MUST rewrite the rtcp attribute if provided.
sections.plainLanguage: If the middle person renames someone, every report card that mentions that person must be corrected too, and the numbers on the cards must still add up.

sections.title: Multiplexing, Reduced-Size RTCP and CNAMEs
sections.content:
For RTP/RTCP multiplexing (RFC 5761), a media-aware B2BUA may use it on one side and not the other. If any party supports it and the B2BUA does too, the rtcp-mux attribute MUST be forwarded. If it uses multiplexing, it MUST make sure no RTP Payload Type numbers conflict, rewriting them and updating the SDP when they do.

For Reduced-Size RTCP (RFC 5506), the RFC discourages enabling it on only one side. It can raise the rate of feedback messages, which could be counterproductive on the side without support. If the feature is not supported by every party, the B2BUA MUST NOT advertise it on either side, by removing rtcp-rsize.

If CNAME-related header extensions are negotiated and the B2BUA changed a CNAME, it MUST update the value there too. A longer CNAME makes the packet larger, which can push it past the MTU and get it dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing one mailbox slot for two kinds of mail only works if the labels do not clash. Shorthand notes should be used by everyone or by no one, so nobody gets flooded with notes they cannot read.

sections.title: Media Terminators
sections.content:
A Media Terminator ends RTP itself, so it produces its own statistics and feedback. Usually there is no end-to-end RTCP exchange between the participants at all, and no extra guideline is needed. If an RTCP message does have to be forwarded, the media-aware rules apply.

RTP/RTCP multiplexing follows the Media Relay guidance. Reduced-Size RTCP is safe to use independently on each side, because the B2BUA terminates RTCP. The B2BUA SHOULD advertise and negotiate it if available, and MUST NOT otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: When the middle person writes all the report cards from scratch, nobody needs the old ones, so the renaming problem mostly goes away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the above assumes the B2BUA can read and change RTP and RTCP. With Secure RTP (SRTP, RFC 3711), a B2BUA without the keys cannot change headers without breaking the packet's hashing, and cannot rewrite RTCP either. So with media security, only the Media Relay scenario can be handled properly. Trying to cover media-aware or terminating cases there makes the B2BUA a man in the middle, and its behaviour is unspecified and discouraged. RFC 7879 has more.

Mishandled RTCP can also resemble an attack. A wrongly handled REMB message about a user's limited bandwidth could lead a peer to raise its encoder bitrate until the user is choked, which looks like a denial-of-service attack. The document needs no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If the report cards are in locked envelopes and the middle person has no key, they cannot fix the names. They can only pass the envelopes along.
